papers.title: The lived experience of trans persons: a bottom-up review co-written by experts by experience and academics.
papers.journal: World psychiatry : official journal of the World Psychiatric Association (WPA)
papers.abstract: We present here the first bottom-up review of the lived experience of trans persons, co-written by experts by experience and academics. We sourced the medical and non-medical literature, focusing on first-person narratives, and critically extracted experiential themes, which were reviewed and appraised in collaborative workshops and eventually shared through a cloud-based system. Numerous experts by experience and academics from diverse gender, ethnic and cultural backgrounds were involved in the above steps and co-wrote the paper. The four overarching themes were: a) the lived experience of trans persons, b) the lived experience of gender affirmation, c) the experience of trans persons in the social and cultural context, and d) the lived experience of receiving care and support. The lived experience of trans persons is characterized by a rich diversity of gender identity experiences, which include identifying as male or female, or simultaneously as male and female and other genders, or as gender fluid. The first-person narratives indicate that common experiences may be of discovering an uncertain gender identity and feeling in the wrong body, together with some degree of mind-body disconnection. However, many trans individuals may feel satisfied with their bodies and identities. The lived experience of gender affirmation includes a process of searching for a bodily and mental redefinition of the self and - at times - fighting oneself to accept one's gender identity. Gender affirmation involves changes in the body to communicate the lived gender identity, as well as behavioral changes. The first-person narrative also highlights the emotional impact of gender affirmation, including the restoration of a sense of self, experiencing a strong emotional reaction to gender-affirming care, and, in a few cases, deciding to stop or reverse gender affirmation. papers.title: From Wartime Nuclear Physics to Isotope Science: George Page and the Foundations of New Zealand Mass Spectrometry.
papers.abstract: The establishment of mass spectrometry in New Zealand coincided with the transition of wartime nuclear physics into civilian research applications in geochemistry, hydrology, geothermal studies, mineral resources and environmental science. George Page (1920-1967) played a central but often overlooked role in New Zealand. Drawing on wartime and post-World War II experience in isotope separation and instrumentation, Page was directly responsible for the construction of New Zealand's first operational mass spectrometer at the Dominion Physical Laboratory. Working with Athol Rafter and Gordon Fergusson, he helped establish the technical capability that supported early radiocarbon dating, stable isotope geochemistry and hydrological studies, including the identification of the post-1954 rise in atmospheric 14C. His work was rarely documented in publications. Instead, his contribution lay in the design and operation of the instruments that made isotope measurements possible with limited resources. This paper examines Page's role through the instruments he developed and shows how they laid the groundwork for isotope science in New Zealand.

papers.title: Social context shapes acoustic signalling in the territorial damselfish Stegastes fuscus.
papers.abstract: Acoustic communication plays an important role in social interactions in reef fishes, but how signals vary with behavioural context remains poorly understood for many species. We characterised the acoustic repertoire of the Brazilian damselfish Stegastes fuscus using synchronised underwater audio-video recordings and tested how sound features vary across social behaviours. Sounds were recorded during agonistic and courtship-related interactions, and temporal and spectral acoustic parameters were measured to compare acoustic structure among contexts. Differences between behaviours were primarily found in temporal features: Courtship sounds were longer and contained more pulses than agonistic sounds. These results show that S. fuscus conveys social context mainly through modulation of temporal organisation rather than spectral properties. Our findings indicate that a single call type can be flexibly adjusted to signal behavioural context during territorial defence and courtship. By documenting the acoustic repertoire of a dominant territorial herbivore, this study highlights how social context structures sound production in damselfishes.

papers.title: Exploring the unspoken: Maternal implicit attitudes and mother-child emotional availability.
papers.abstract: The quality of the mother-child bond is vital to children's socioemotional development. A mother's attitude toward her child might be especially important in this regard; however, assessing such attitudes is difficult given strong reporting biases in close relationships and especially mother-child relationships. Implicit attitudes-thought to reflect the summary of evaluative associations developed through personal experiences with a (close) other-may be one way to circumvent such biases. We investigated the link between mothers' implicit attitudes about her child and the quality of the mother-child bond, indexed by mothers' and their child's behavior during a dyadic interaction. Child sex (male/female) was also evaluated as the dynamics of mother-son and mother-daughter dyads can differ. Between 2012 and 2015, mother-child dyads (N = 217) were recruited from a longitudinal study; dyads were videotaped during a free-play interaction, and their behavior was coded for emotional availability (EA). Mothers completed the MyChild Implicit Association Test indexing their implicit attitudes toward their child. Maternal implicit attitudes were positively associated with mothers' EA, an effect driven by mother-son dyads; these effects held when controlling for child behavior, supporting the unique role of implicit attitudes in guiding mothers' EA. Regarding the child's EA (responsivity, inclusion), mother-son and mother-daughter dyads showed the opposite pattern: Maternal implicit attitudes were positively associated with sons' EA but negatively associated with daughters' EA. These findings highlight the importance of implicit attitudes in the mother-child relationship and are among the few to link implicit attitudes to the attitude target's behavior. papers.title: More Than Hurt Feelings: Associations Between Perceived Racial Discrimination and Mental Health, Substance Use, and Victimization Among Racial and Ethnic Minority Adolescents.
papers.journal: Journal of racial and ethnic health disparities
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Although prior research has linked perceived racial discrimination (PRD) to adverse outcomes among adolescents, fewer studies have comprehensively examined its associations with mental health, substance use, and victimization outcomes within a single nationally representative sample. The objective of this study is to examine the associations between school-based interpersonal PRD and a broad range of mental health, substance use, and victimization outcomes among racial/ethnic minority adolescents in the United States. METHODS: Data for this study were obtained from the 2023 Youth Risk Behavior Survey. The analytic sample included 9,885 racial/ethnic minority adolescents aged 14-18 (50.7% male). The associations between school-based interpersonal PRD and twenty-two outcomes spanning mental health (n = 6), current substance use (n = 6), and victimization and violence-related experiences (n = 10) were examined using binary logistic regression. RESULTS: We found that 16.7% of adolescents reported sometimes experiencing school-based interpersonal PRD and 6.9% experienced PRD most of the time or always. In the multivariable logistic regression models, adolescents who experienced school-based interpersonal PRD most of the time or always had higher odds of poor mental health, sadness or hopelessness, suicidal ideation, suicide planning, and suicide attempts (adjusted odds ratios [AORs] = 3.39-5.19) compared to adolescents who never experienced PRD. The strongest associations were observed for victimization outcomes, including school bullying (AOR = 9.68), being threatened or injured on school property (AOR = 8.44), and physical dating violence (AOR = 7.68). CONCLUSIONS: School-based interpersonal PRD was associated with mental health problems, substance use, and victimization among racial/ethnic minority adolescents. papers.title: Analyzing model inaccuracy and relative importance of parameters of discrete model of adhesion of circulating tumor cells for investigating metastatic dynamics.
papers.abstract: Metastasis is strongly influenced by the ability of cancerous cells to adhere to endothelial cells, facilitating their extravasation to distant organs; however, how uncertainty in cellular and adhesion properties propagates to observable dynamics remains unclear. A key finding is that a physiological "speed limit" imposed by Poiseuille flow fundamentally constrains this uncertainty: although input variability reaches a coefficient of variation (CV) of 20%, the resulting variability in CTC velocity saturates at ∼12%, revealing a bounded, nonlinear response rather than a linear error amplification. Coupling the stochastic LBM-DEM-IBM adhesive dynamic model with a high-fidelity Random Forest surrogate enables time-resolved global sensitivity analysis (Sobol' and E-FAST). This coupled model shows that parameter importance is stage-dependent: early attachment is dominated by membrane/link elasticity, whereas stable rolling is governed by bond spring stiffness and rupture mechanics. These insights explain why velocity variability attenuates while adhesion outcomes can still diverge (rolling vs detachment). In contrast, adhesion behavior remains highly sensitive to parameter variability. Machine learning (XGBoost) enables accurate classification of CTC rolling or detachment states with 95.62% accuracy, providing a predictive framework for assessing detachment likelihood under uncertainty. Together, these results establish a unified physics-to-mechanism perspective in which flow-imposed limits, stage-dependent control, and sparse parameter interactions govern CTC adhesion dynamics to enhance predictive models for metastasis.

papers.title: Dyadic coping affect mothers' and fathers' depressive symptoms during pregnancy.
papers.journal: Journal of reproductive and infant psychology
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to explore whether dyadic coping strategies are associated with both women's and men's depressive symptoms during pregnancy. BACKGROUND: Very few studies have investigated the association between dyadic coping and depressive symptoms in couples during the transition to parenthood. METHODS: A sample of 192 couples completed the Dyadic Coping Inventory and Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale. The data were analysed using regression and the actor-partner interdependence model. RESULTS: Three actor effects and two partner effects were found for depressive symptoms in women, and five actor effects and five partner effects were found for depressive symptoms in men. Men's depressive symptoms were associated with less supportive dyadic coping in men, less delegated dyadic coping in men, as reported by both partners, less common dyadic coping, as reported by men, and lower evaluation of dyadic coping (EDC), as reported by both partners. Men's depressive symptoms were also linked to more negative dyadic coping (NDC) in women, as reported by both partners. Women's depressive symptoms were associated with lower stress communication in men, as reported by both partners, less delegated dyadic coping in men, as reported by men, and lower EDC and higher NDC in men, as reported by women. CONCLUSION: Women's and men's dyadic coping affect their own and their partner's depressive symptoms, which highlights the necessity of early screening for both partners. Early detection would enable the implementation of targeted interventions to support dyadic coping.

papers.title: Honoring Children's Communication Rights: Listening to the Perspectives of Children Who Stutter Using Drawings, Self-Report Measures, and Interviews.
papers.journal: Language, speech, and hearing services in schools
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: Reflecting a commitment to the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC), and Articles 12 (respect for children's views) and Article 13 (sharing thoughts freely) in particular, this study aimed to explore whether drawings with interviews are a suitable method for understanding the perspectives of children who stutter (CWS) and what CWS communicate about their talking using this method. METHOD: Data were collected with 16 children aged 4;0 (years;months)-6;10 and involved drawings (62), interviews, and three self-report measures. The drawings were analyzed quantitatively across two dimensions: (a) developmental analysis and (b) focal point analysis. Inductive reflexive thematic analysis of the interview transcripts was also conducted. RESULTS: Self-report measure scores indicated that most participants were "happy" about their talking with an average self-perception of little/no difficulty when talking. Participants demonstrated developmentally age-appropriate drawing skills. Six focal points were identified across the 62 drawings: (1) facial expressions, (2) accentuation of body features, (3) portrayal of talking/listening, (4) colors used, (5) conversation partners, and (6) sense of self. Four themes were generated: (1) familial relationships, (2) friendship, (3) child's interests, and (4) self-perception of competence. CONCLUSIONS: Drawing with an interview is a suitable method for understanding the perspectives of CWS. A range of perspectives were expressed by the children. Stuttering was not found to be a prominent feature of children's perspectives on their talking. These findings contribute to the adoption of holistic, person-centered approaches when working with CWS in speech-language pathology.

papers.title: Revisiting nostalgia for current and ex-romantic partners: Affective profiles and the moderating effect of relationship duration.
papers.abstract: Nostalgia is a self-relevant, socially grounded emotion marked by a sentimental longing for the past. Compared to the well-documented benefits known about general personal nostalgia, most nostalgia studies in both emotion and relationship science rely heavily on Western samples, and nostalgic effects of former partners are mixed. With an Asian sample, the present research had two main aims: (a) Experimentally replicate the nostalgic effects of current and ex-partners on current relationship quality, and (b) examine the moderating role of relationship duration. Results revealed both ex- and romantic nostalgia increased relationship satisfaction, and, more interestingly, romantic nostalgia decreased relationship commitment in shorter relationships. Furthermore, exploratory analyses highlighted distinct affective patterns within romantic nostalgia. Implications and contributions are further discussed. papers.title: Intimate Partner Violence During Pregnancy in Mansoura, Egypt: Medico-Legal and Psychological Points of View.
papers.abstract: Intimate partner violence during pregnancy is a significant health concern. This prospective cohort study aimed to estimate prevalence and examine associations with adverse obstetric and psychological outcomes in an Egyptian community. 2,292 pregnant women completed the NorVold Domestic Abuse Questionnaire and Hamilton Depression Rating Scale. 42.15% reported IPV: emotional (67.7%), physical (58.4%), and sexual (43.7%). Adverse pregnancy outcomes: abortion, rupture of membranes, fetal distress/death, and low birth weight, were found to be more frequent among exposed participants (p < .05). Higher depressive symptom scores were significantly associated with greater severity of physical (p = .042) and sexual violence (p = .038).

papers.title: A Realist Evaluation of a Behavior Change Program for Domestic Abuse Perpetrators in the United Kingdom.
papers.abstract: The Behavior Change Independent Domestic Violence Advisor Program is a Domestic Abuse Perpetrator Program operating in England. This evaluation drew upon semistructured interviews with program professionals (n = 7), perpetrators (n = 7) and victims/survivors (n = 5) to develop a realist model of how perpetrator behavior change is thought to be enabled through this program. Key contextual factors were identified which moderate program delivery and lead to the conditions required to initiate six mechanisms of change which could lead to outcomes of a reduction in abusive behaviors, reoffending, and harm to victims/survivors.

papers.title: Prevalence and sources of gender-based violence among female youth in Jordan: An egocentric social network study.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Previous literature emphasized that females with different age-groups are subjected to psychological, physical, and sexual abuse. There are many possible sources of violence against females including intimate partners, parents, family members, cousins, neighbors, and any man with authority or power. OBJECTIVE: To explore the prevalence and sources of different violence acts among the Jordanian female youth (18-24 years). DESIGN: A cross-sectional, egocentric social network design was used to collect data from 960 youth in Jordan (480 men and 480 women) aged between 18 years and 24 years. While 437 female youth participated in the broader survey, the analytic sample for intimate partner violence acts was restricted to 171 ever-married or in-relationship youth. A convenience sample was recruited via four community centres located in East Amman. FINDINGS: The prevalence of lifetime control violence was 75% (128), psychological violence was 39.8% (68), and physical and sexual violence was 15.2%. Control and psychological violence are the most prevalent forms of abuse faced by Jordanian female youth. 19.9% of women reported exposure to family violence. Additionally, 35% of these women reported being abused as children. Participants who experienced abusive acts were more likely to be exposed to bullying χ2 (1, N = 171) = 10.33, p < .001, and verbal harassment from strangers χ2 (1, N = 171) = 13.01, p < .001. Participants who experienced abusive acts were more likely to be suffering from financial difficulties and insufficient income χ2 (3, N = 171) = 8.66, p = .04. CONCLUSION: Addressing GBV among young women in Jordan necessitates a multifaceted approach that involves legislative reforms, awareness campaigns, and the provision of support services tailored to the specific needs of this demographic. papers.title: "They Looked at Me Like I Was Crazy": Practitioner Experiences Among People Engaging in Hair-Pulling.
papers.abstract: Trichotillomania is a disorder affecting 1-2% of the population during their lifetime and is characterised by recurrent hair-pulling that often leads to distress, low self-esteem, social ostracism, and lowered relationship satisfaction. Despite the availability of effective therapies, individuals with trichotillomania frequently report dissatisfaction with clinical care. This qualitative study explored the experiences of 20 adults with trichotillomania, focusing on their interactions with mental health practitioners. Using reflexive thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews, we constructed two themes: feeling (mis)understood and therapeutic (dis)connections. Participants described significant challenges in finding knowledgeable, compassionate practitioners, often encountering practitioners with dismissive attitudes, inaccurate assumptions, or misunderstanding of their condition. A common frustration involved practitioners conflating hair-pulling with self-harm, which many participants viewed as invalidating. However, some participants reported supportive therapeutic relationships that fostered acceptance and coping. Positive experiences were marked by practitioner empathy, validation, and tailored advice. These findings highlight the critical role of therapeutic alliance and practitioner compassion in treatment satisfaction and engagement. Greater awareness of trichotillomania and sensitivity to individuals' explanatory models among practitioners are essential for improving clinical outcomes.
